questionBank.question: Study 1: What is Christianity centered on?

choices.text: Jesus Christ—who he is, what he did, and the life of following him
A modern self-improvement program
One particular nation or political party
A system for earning God's favor through perfect behavior

questionBank.explanation: John 20:30–31 says the recorded signs were written so readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name. First Corinthians 15:1–5 summarizes the gospel around Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances. “Christ” translates G5547, Christos, a title meaning Anointed One and corresponding to Messiah; it is not Jesus' surname. Saying Christianity centers on Jesus is a summary of these passages and the broader New Testament witness.

questionBank.question: Study 2: What is the Bible?

choices.text: A collection of writings through which Christians receive the scriptural witness to God and his work
A single book written at one sitting
Only a list of rules
A replacement for God

questionBank.explanation: Second Timothy 3:14–17 says the sacred writings make a person wise unto salvation through faith in Christ and are profitable for teaching, correction, and instruction in righteousness. The Bible contains history, law, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, Gospel, letters, and apocalyptic vision, so each passage should be read according to its context and literary form. Jesus and the New Testament writers repeatedly use Israel's Scriptures. Different Christian traditions arrange or include some Old Testament writings differently, while all major Christian traditions receive the same twenty-seven New Testament books. A later module can examine the history of the biblical canon in greater detail. Canon history is descriptive background, while the authority claimed in 2 Timothy must be examined from the text itself.

questionBank.question: Study 3: How should a beginner read Scripture?

choices.text: Read passages in context, notice their kind of writing, and compare them with the Bible's larger message
Open randomly and treat the first line as a private prediction
Ignore the surrounding chapter
Assume every sentence is addressed directly to the same audience

questionBank.explanation: Acts 17:10–12 praises the Bereans for receiving the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to test it. Good reading also observes the features already present in a text: speaker, audience, setting, purpose, and literary form. A proverb functions differently from a narrative report, parable, or command in a letter. Strong's numbers can help locate original-language entries, but a short gloss cannot override grammar, context, or usage elsewhere in Scripture.

questionBank.question: Study 4: What does Scripture teach about God?

choices.text: There is one God, the Creator and Lord of all
God is merely another name for the universe
Many rival gods created different parts of reality
God is only a human idea with no claim on life

questionBank.explanation: Genesis 1:1 says God created the heavens and the earth. Deuteronomy 6:4 confesses that Jehovah is one. Scripture describes God as holy, just, loving, faithful, merciful, and worthy of worship. Strong's H430, Elohim, is a common Hebrew designation translated “God”; H3068 indexes the covenant name printed “Jehovah” in the ASV. These word entries help locate usage but do not supply a complete doctrine by themselves. Because creation belongs to God, Scripture presents human beings as accountable to him.

questionBank.question: Study 5: What does it mean that humans bear God's image?

choices.text: Human beings have God-given dignity and are called to represent his rule within creation
God has an ordinary human body
Only rulers and religious leaders possess human worth
People are divine by nature

questionBank.explanation: Genesis 1:26–28 says God created humanity in his image, male and female, and gave them responsibility within creation. Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 continue to appeal to God's image or likeness. Scripture does not provide one dictionary-style explanation of the image. Interpretations emphasize representation, relationship, moral capacity, rule, or combinations of these. The text clearly gives humanity a distinctive God-given calling and forbids treating other image-bearers as worthless.

questionBank.question: Study 6: What is the Trinity?

choices.text: The Christian confession of one God who is eternally Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Three separate gods cooperating together
One person changing costumes at different times
A claim that Jesus is the Father

questionBank.explanation: Deuteronomy 6:4 says God is one. Matthew 3:16–17 distinguishes the Son, the descending Spirit, and the Father's voice. Matthew 28:19 joins Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the singular “name.” John 1:1–18, John 14–16, and Acts 5:3–4 add further evidence. “Trinity” is a later, uninspired theological label for the interpretation that these passages teach one God in three personally distinct persons. The label and formulation must be tested by Scripture; they are not substitutes for reading the passages.

questionBank.question: Study 7: Who is Jesus?

choices.text: The eternal Word who became truly human, the Son of God and promised Christ
Only a symbol with no historical life
A created angel who merely appeared human
A teacher whose identity is unimportant to Christianity

questionBank.explanation: John 1:1 says the Word was with God and was God, and John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Philippians 2:5–11 and Hebrews 2:14–18 should be read alongside it. Strong's G3056, logos, can mean word, message, or expression; in John 1 the evangelist uses it as a title. “Fully divine and fully human” and “incarnation” are later summaries intended to preserve the combined claims of these passages, not inspired wording. Students should evaluate the summaries from the texts.

questionBank.question: Study 8: What did Jesus teach about God's kingdom?

choices.text: God's saving rule had drawn near, calling people to repent, believe, and live as his people
God's kingdom was only a new earthly political party
The kingdom meant people no longer needed mercy
The kingdom had nothing to do with daily conduct

questionBank.explanation: Mark 1:14–15 records Jesus announcing that the time was fulfilled, God's kingdom was at hand, and hearers should repent and believe the gospel. The Gospels connect the kingdom with Jesus' teaching, authority, forgiveness, healings, deliverance, death, and resurrection. “God's saving rule” is an explanatory summary rather than the wording of one verse. The parables portray both present and future aspects, and each kingdom passage should be read in its own context before constructing a timetable.

questionBank.question: Study 9: Why are Jesus' death and resurrection central?

choices.text: Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised, defeating death and grounding Christian hope
They are optional details added after Jesus' teaching
They teach that physical life is evil
They mean Jesus never truly suffered or died

questionBank.explanation: First Corinthians 15:3–8 states that Christ died for sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to witnesses. Paul argues through the rest of the chapter that if Christ has not been raised, preaching and faith are vain, and he connects Christ's resurrection with the future resurrection of the dead. Other passages explain the cross through sacrifice, ransom, reconciliation, covenant, example, and victory. The primary facts should be learned from the passages before adopting a later atonement model.

questionBank.question: Study 10: What is sin?

choices.text: Rebellion against God and failure to live in faithful love toward God and neighbor
Only mistakes that cause public embarrassment
A problem affecting only unusually cruel people
Merely having a physical body

questionBank.explanation: Romans 1:18–3:23 argues that both Gentiles and Jews are under sin and concludes that all have sinned. Scripture also speaks of lawlessness (1 John 3:4), failure to do known good (James 4:17), corrupt desires, unbelief, transgression, slavery, and death. G266, hamartia, is commonly translated sin, but the popular shorthand “missing the mark” does not capture every biblical use. The answer summarizes this range and should be tested against the full passages.

questionBank.question: Study 11: What is the result of sin?

choices.text: Alienation from God, corruption, judgment, and death
No lasting consequence if a person means well
Only a loss of social reputation
Automatic spiritual growth

questionBank.explanation: Romans 6:15–23 describes sin as a master and says its wages are death, while God's gift is eternal life in Christ. Ephesians 2:1–5 speaks of being dead through trespasses and made alive with Christ. Other passages use additional images, but no one image should be treated as the entire doctrine. Scripture clearly connects sin with bondage, judgment, and death while announcing mercy and life through Christ.

questionBank.question: Study 12: Can good works erase sin or place God in our debt?

choices.text: No. Good works matter, but salvation is God's gift rather than a wage God owes us
Yes, if good acts slightly outnumber bad acts
Yes, because motives never matter
No, therefore Christian conduct is completely irrelevant

questionBank.explanation: Ephesians 2:8–10 says salvation is by grace through faith, not from works for boasting, and immediately says those saved are created in Christ Jesus for good works. Titus 3:3–8 similarly moves from God's mercy to devotion to good works. Romans 3–4, Galatians 2–3, and James 2 should be compared rather than used to cancel one another. Traditions explain the relationship among grace, faith, obedience, and final judgment differently; the clear starting point is God's mercy rather than a claim that God owes salvation for independent human merit.

questionBank.question: Study 13: What does “gospel” mean?

choices.text: Good news—the announcement of what God has done through Jesus Christ
Advice for becoming wealthy
A secret code available only to experts
A general command to try harder

questionBank.explanation: Strong's G2098, euangelion, means good news or good tidings. Mark 1:14–15 connects the gospel with God's kingdom and calls for repentance and belief. First Corinthians 15:1–5 summarizes the message around Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances. Romans 1:16 calls the gospel God's power unto salvation to everyone who believes. Saying it is “news before advice” is commentary emphasizing that these texts announce God's action before describing the human response.

questionBank.question: Study 14: What is grace?

choices.text: God's undeserved favor and generous action toward people who cannot save themselves
God pretending sin is harmless
A reward paid to people who never fail
Permission to continue deliberately in evil

questionBank.explanation: G5485, charis, is commonly translated grace and may carry ideas of favor, gift, or graciousness according to context. Romans 3:21–26 speaks of being justified freely by God's grace through redemption in Christ; Romans 6:1–14 rejects continuing in sin as a proper response to grace; Titus 2:11–14 says grace instructs toward godly living. Saying justice and mercy meet at the cross is a theological summary of these texts, not the wording of a single verse.

questionBank.question: Study 15: What is salvation?

choices.text: God's rescue of people from sin and death into reconciliation, new life, and final restoration in Christ
Only escaping an unpleasant feeling
Becoming morally superior to everyone else
A promise that believers will avoid all earthly suffering

questionBank.explanation: The New Testament uses salvation language in past, present, and future settings: Ephesians 2:8 says believers have been saved; 1 Corinthians 1:18 speaks of those being saved; Romans 13:11 says salvation is nearer. Scripture also speaks of forgiveness, justification, reconciliation, adoption, redemption, renewal, and resurrection. Strong's G4991, soteria, refers to rescue, safety, or salvation, but context determines what aspect is in view. The broad summary in this answer should be checked against each cited passage.

questionBank.question: Study 16: What is repentance?

choices.text: A God-directed change of mind and life: turning from sin toward God
Feeling embarrassed without changing direction
Punishing oneself until forgiveness is earned
Blaming other people for one's choices

questionBank.explanation: Mark 1:15 joins repentance with believing the gospel. Luke 3:7–14 calls for fruit worthy of repentance, and Acts 3:19 calls hearers to repent and turn so sins may be blotted out. G3341, metanoia, is translated repentance, but a word gloss alone cannot establish the doctrine. These passages show more than embarrassment: they describe a God-directed turn expressed in changed conduct.

questionBank.question: Study 17: What is saving faith?

choices.text: Trusting and relying on Jesus Christ in a way that receives God's promise and reorients one's allegiance
Merely knowing that Christians exist
Confidence in one's own moral record
Believing without any concern for whom one trusts

questionBank.explanation: Acts 16:31 calls the jailer to believe on the Lord Jesus. Romans 10:8–13 connects belief with the proclaimed word and confession of Jesus as Lord. James 2:14–26 warns that a claimed faith without works is dead. G4102, pistis, can mean faith, belief, trust, or faithfulness according to context. “Saving faith” is a study label, and traditions explain faith's relationship to obedience differently; students should read each author's full argument.

questionBank.question: Study 18: What is baptism?

choices.text: The water rite Jesus commanded for disciples, identifying them with Christ and his people
A private achievement unrelated to the church
A guarantee that no future spiritual growth is needed
A substitute for faith, repentance, and following Jesus

questionBank.explanation: Matthew 28:18–20 records Jesus commanding disciples to baptize. Acts repeatedly records baptism in response to the gospel. Acts 2:38 connects baptism with repentance, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit; Romans 6:3–4 connects it with Christ's death and newness of life; 1 Peter 3:21 connects it with an appeal to God through Jesus' resurrection. Christians differ over infant or professing-believer baptism, mode, and how baptism relates to regeneration, forgiveness, faith, and assurance. This introduction presents all these passages and does not use one to silence the others.

questionBank.question: Study 19: Who is the Holy Spirit?

choices.text: The divine Spirit who gives life, dwells in believers, forms holiness, and empowers witness
Only an impersonal name for human enthusiasm
A rival god opposed to the Father and Son
A power Christians control for personal status

questionBank.explanation: John 14–16 portrays the Spirit teaching, reminding, bearing witness, convicting, guiding, and glorifying Christ. Acts 5:3–4 places lying to the Holy Spirit in parallel with lying to God. First Corinthians 12 says the Spirit distributes gifts as he wills, and Galatians 5:22–23 names the Spirit's fruit. Calling the Spirit personal and divine is an interpretation drawn from these combined statements. Students should examine the passages themselves and distinguish their wording from the summary.

questionBank.question: Study 20: What place do love and obedience have in Christian life?

choices.text: They are the fruit of receiving God's love and following Jesus, not a way to make grace unnecessary
They are irrelevant once someone says they believe
They earn the right to look down on others
They apply only during church services

questionBank.explanation: Matthew 22:34–40 records Jesus joining love for God with love for neighbor. John 13:34–35 commands disciples to love one another as Jesus loved them, and 1 John 4:7–21 grounds love in God's prior love. G26, agape, is commonly translated love, but its content comes from usage and context rather than an automatic special meaning. Describing obedience as a response to grace is a synthesis that should be compared with John 14–15, Romans 12, and 1 John.

questionBank.question: Study 21: What are prayer and spiritual practices for?

choices.text: Communion with God and formation into faithful love, trust, worship, and obedience
Manipulating God into granting every request
Displaying spiritual superiority
Avoiding responsibility for wise action

questionBank.explanation: Matthew 6:1–18 warns against practicing piety for display and teaches prayer for God's name and kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance. Philippians 4:4–7 connects prayer and thanksgiving with bringing requests to God, and 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 commands continual prayer and thanksgiving. “Communion with God and formation” is explanatory language summarizing these practices; it is not a claim that the practices earn God's favor.

questionBank.question: Study 22: What is the church?

choices.text: The community of people called by God in Christ to worship, learn, serve, witness, and share life together
Only a building used once a week
A group where leaders are never accountable
An optional audience for otherwise isolated Christians

questionBank.explanation: Acts 2:37–47 describes believers continuing in apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers, shared care, praise, and witness. First Corinthians 12 calls believers Christ's body, and Ephesians 2 calls them God's household and a holy temple. G1577, ekklesia, commonly means assembly or congregation. “The church is people before property” summarizes these biblical images; it does not settle disputed questions of church government.

questionBank.question: Study 23: What is the Lord's Supper?

choices.text: The meal Jesus gave the church to remember and proclaim his death and share in communion with him and one another
A celebration of human self-sufficiency
A replacement for reconciliation and love within the church
A practice with no connection to Jesus' death

questionBank.explanation: Luke 22:14–20 connects the bread and cup with Jesus' body and new-covenant blood and commands remembrance. First Corinthians 10:16–17 speaks of communion or participation in Christ's blood and body and connects one loaf with one body. First Corinthians 11:23–26 says the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes. Traditions differ over Christ's presence, sacramental or ordinance language, admission, and frequency. The undisputed starting point is the wording and context of these passages.

questionBank.question: Study 24: What is the Christian hope?

choices.text: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, evil will be judged, and God's creation will be made new
Human beings will solve death by moral effort alone
Creation will always remain under death with no final justice
Only the present moment matters

questionBank.explanation: First Corinthians 15 teaches Christ's resurrection and the future resurrection of the dead. First Thessalonians 4:13–18 connects hope with Christ's coming. Revelation 20 describes judgment, and Revelation 21–22 depicts a new heaven and earth, God's dwelling with humanity, and death removed. Christians differ over the chronology and symbolism of some end-times passages. This question affirms the shared conclusions directly stated across the cited texts without imposing one detailed system.

questionBank.question: How do the Old and New Testaments relate to one another?

choices.text: The New Testament continues the story begun in the Old Testament and presents Jesus as the fulfillment of God's saving promises
The New Testament says the Old Testament has no value
They describe two unrelated gods
The Old Testament was written after the New Testament

questionBank.explanation: Luke 24:25–27 and 44–49 records Jesus interpreting Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms in relation to his suffering, resurrection, repentance, and forgiveness. Romans 15:4 says earlier writings were written for instruction and hope. The conclusion that the Testaments form one unfolding account is a canonical interpretation based on how New Testament writers use Israel's Scriptures. It must not erase an Old Testament passage's original literary and historical setting.

questionBank.question: What are the four New Testament Gospels?

choices.text: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—four accounts bearing witness to Jesus' life, teaching, death, and resurrection
Four letters written by Paul
Four different religions about unrelated people
A complete biography of every year of Jesus' earthly life

questionBank.explanation: Luke 1:1–4 says many had undertaken narratives and that Luke wrote an orderly account after tracing matters carefully. John 20:30–31 says John selected signs for a stated purpose. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John overlap but also select and arrange material differently. “Synoptic Gospels” is a later study label for Matthew, Mark, and Luke because of their extensive similarities; it is useful terminology, not inspired vocabulary.

questionBank.question: What does it mean that God is holy?

choices.text: God is utterly set apart from evil, morally pure, and worthy of reverent worship
God is distant and incapable of love
God approves whatever people prefer
God's character changes whenever culture changes

questionBank.explanation: Isaiah 6:1–8 portrays Jehovah as king and “holy, holy, holy,” exposes Isaiah's uncleanness, provides cleansing, and sends him. First Peter 1:13–16 calls believers to holiness because God is holy. Strong's H6918, qadosh, and G40, hagios, are commonly translated holy, but the passages—not a gloss alone—show how holiness relates to God's majesty, moral purity, cleansing, and the calling of his people.

questionBank.question: What is providence?

choices.text: God's continuing care for and governance of creation as he works toward his good purposes
The belief that creation now exists outside God's concern
A promise that believers will never suffer
A technique for predicting every event

questionBank.explanation: Matthew 6:25–34 points to the Father's care for birds and flowers and commands disciples to seek God's kingdom rather than be ruled by anxiety. Romans 8:28–39 speaks of God's purpose, suffering, and inseparable love in Christ. “Providence” is a later summary term for biblical teaching about God's care and governance, not an inspired word. Christians differ over how divine sovereignty and human choice relate; this question does not settle that debate.

questionBank.question: What is the incarnation?

choices.text: The eternal Son truly became human without ceasing to be divine
Jesus only appeared to have a body
A human teacher later replaced God
The Father stopped being God and became Jesus

questionBank.explanation: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Philippians 2:5–11 and Hebrews 2:14–18 describe Christ's divine status, servant form, human likeness, shared flesh and blood, suffering, and death. “Incarnation” is a later theological label meaning becoming flesh. “Truly divine and truly human” is an interpretive summary intended to preserve the combined claims of these passages, and students should test it by reading them directly.

questionBank.question: What does the New Testament teach that Jesus accomplished through the cross?

choices.text: He dealt with sin, reconciled sinners to God, defeated hostile powers, and demonstrated God's self-giving love
Only that suffering has no meaning
That God no longer cares about justice
That people can save themselves by copying one brave act

questionBank.explanation: The New Testament describes Christ's death through several images: ransom (Mark 10:45), sacrifice and justification (Romans 3:21–26), reconciliation (Colossians 1:19–22), victory over hostile powers (Colossians 2:13–15), and example with sin-bearing (1 Peter 2:21–25). Christians organize these texts into atonement explanations differently. The module does not declare one later model complete at the expense of the others.

questionBank.question: What is justification?

choices.text: God's gracious setting right of sinners through Jesus Christ, described in passages such as Romans 3–5
A claim that sin was never wrong
A reward for people who have made themselves flawless
The same thing as never needing spiritual growth

questionBank.explanation: G1344, dikaioo, is translated justify and can carry declarative or vindicatory senses according to context. Romans 3:21–28 connects justification with God's grace, Christ's redemption, faith, and the exclusion of boasting; Romans 5:1–2 connects it with peace and access. Traditions differ over whether justification should be described only as a changed standing or also in relation to inward renewal, sacraments, obedience, and final judgment. Students should compare Romans, Galatians, and James before adopting a system.

questionBank.question: What is reconciliation?

choices.text: The restoration of a broken relationship, especially peace between God and sinners through Christ
Ignoring hostility while leaving it unchanged
Proving that humans were never alienated from God
Earning control over another person

questionBank.explanation: Romans 5:6–11 says people who were enemies were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. Second Corinthians 5:14–21 says God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ and entrusted the message of reconciliation. G2643, katallage, is translated reconciliation. Applying reconciliation to human relationships is a broader biblical implication that should be tested alongside Matthew 5:23–24, Matthew 18:15–35, Romans 12:14–21, and passages concerning justice and truth.

questionBank.question: What is adoption in Christian teaching?

choices.text: God welcomes believers into his family as sons and daughters with a new identity and inheritance
A claim that every believer becomes the eternal Son by nature
Only a legal metaphor with no effect on Christian life
A reward restricted to one ethnicity

questionBank.explanation: Romans 8:12–17 says those led by the Spirit are children of God, cry “Abba, Father,” and are heirs with Christ. Galatians 4:4–7 uses adoption language similarly, and Ephesians 1:3–6 connects adoption with God's purpose in Christ. The description of belonging, access, and inheritance summarizes these texts. Adoption does not say believers become divine or become sons in the unique sense in which Jesus is the Son.

questionBank.question: What is confession?

choices.text: Truthfully acknowledging sin before God and, where appropriate, before those affected
Making excuses until responsibility disappears
Publicly revealing every private matter to everyone
Punishing oneself so God must forgive

questionBank.explanation: Psalm 32 connects acknowledged sin with forgiveness. First John 1:5–10 connects confession with God's faithfulness to forgive and cleanse, and James 5:16 speaks of confessing sins to one another and praying for one another. The guidance about appropriate disclosure and repair is pastoral application rather than a direct quotation. It should be practiced with wisdom, truth, safety, and attention to passages about restitution and reconciliation.

questionBank.question: What is discipleship?

choices.text: Learning from Jesus and ordering one's whole life under his teaching and lordship
Collecting religious facts without following Jesus
A program only for professional clergy
A promise of comfort without sacrifice

questionBank.explanation: Luke 9:23–26 records Jesus calling followers to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him. Luke 14:25–33 stresses counting the cost, and Matthew 28:18–20 commands making disciples, baptizing, and teaching obedience to Jesus' commands. “Discipleship” is a study term for this pattern of learning and following. Ephesians 2:8–10 should be read alongside these texts so costly obedience is not confused with earning God's grace.

questionBank.question: What is sanctification?

choices.text: God's work of setting believers apart and transforming them into holy, Christlike people
Instant moral perfection that removes every struggle
Self-improvement without the Holy Spirit
Separation from everyone who is not already mature

questionBank.explanation: First Corinthians 1:2 speaks of believers as sanctified in Christ and called saints. First Thessalonians 4:1–8 calls believers to continuing sanctification, and 2 Corinthians 3:18 speaks of transformation. G38, hagiasmos, is translated sanctification or holiness. “Already set apart and progressively transformed” is a summary of these uses. Traditions differ over the process and possible degree of holiness; the passages should govern the conclusion.

questionBank.question: Why do Christians study Scripture?

choices.text: To know God and his saving work, be formed in truth, test teaching, and be equipped for faithful living
To collect isolated sentences that support any opinion
To avoid applying truth to personal conduct
To replace prayer, community, and wisdom

questionBank.explanation: Psalm 1 describes delight and meditation in God's law. Acts 17:10–12 praises examination of Scripture, and 2 Timothy 3:14–17 says the sacred writings give wisdom unto salvation and equip for every good work. Careful reading, context, meditation, and comparison are methods serving those aims. Teachers and study tools may help, but Acts 17:11 provides the model for testing claims rather than accepting them merely because an authority states them.

questionBank.question: What is Christian worship?

choices.text: The response of the whole person and gathered church to God's worth through praise, prayer, truth, obedience, and service
Only a particular style of music
Entertainment designed around the audience
A weekly activity unrelated to ordinary life

questionBank.explanation: John 4:19–24 records Jesus teaching worship in spirit and truth. Romans 12:1–2 describes presenting the body as a living sacrifice and calls it spiritual service or worship. Acts 2:42 names apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers. The broader description in the answer gathers these biblical practices; it does not prescribe one denomination's service order or one musical style.

questionBank.question: Why does the Holy Spirit give spiritual gifts?

choices.text: For service, witness, and building up the church for the common good
To prove that gifted people are more valuable than others
To eliminate the need for love and character
To give one person every role in the church

questionBank.explanation: First Corinthians 12 says manifestations of the Spirit are given for the common good and compares the congregation to a body of many necessary members. Chapters 13–14 require love, edification, and order. Romans 12:3–8 and 1 Peter 4:10–11 add further gifts and service. Christians differ over whether every gift continues in the same form today. The passages clearly reject superiority and direct gifts toward serving others.

questionBank.question: What does final judgment affirm?

choices.text: God will expose truth, judge evil justly, vindicate his purposes, and bring history to its appointed end through Christ
God is indifferent to injustice
Humans may safely judge their own lives by comparison alone
Christian hope has no concern for what people do

questionBank.explanation: Acts 17:30–31 says God commands repentance and has appointed a day to judge through the risen Jesus. Romans 2:1–16 speaks of impartial judgment, and Revelation 20:11–15 depicts the final judgment. Christians debate details of sequence, symbolism, and the final state, but Scripture clearly presents divine judgment, resurrection, Christ's return, and God's final victory. This answer does not select a detailed end-times chronology.

lessons.title: Beginning with Jesus
lessons.summary: Christianity begins with Jesus Christ and the biblical witness to him.

sections.heading: Scripture Reading — ASV
sections.content:
Read the biblical text first. The explanatory sections that follow are commentary and should be tested against these passages.

Mark 1:1 (ASV)

1. The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

Luke 1:1–4 (ASV)

1. Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to draw up a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,

2. even as they delivered them unto us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word,

3. it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus;

4. that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.

John 20:30–31 (ASV)

30. Many other signs therefore did Jesus in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book:

31. but these are written, that ye may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye may have life in his name.

2 Timothy 3:14–17 (ASV)

14. But abide thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;

15. and that from a babe thou hast known the sacred writings which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

16. Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction which is in righteousness:

sections.heading: The Center
sections.content: The cited passages place Jesus Christ at the center of the message. John 20:31 states that its recorded signs were written so readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name. “Christ” translates G5547, Christos, a title meaning Anointed One and corresponding to Messiah; it is not Jesus' surname. The explanation that Christianity centers on Jesus summarizes these texts rather than replacing them.

sections.heading: The Scriptures
sections.content: Second Timothy 3:14–17 says the sacred writings make a person wise unto salvation through faith in Christ and are profitable for teaching, correction, and instruction. The Bible contains many literary forms, so responsible reading asks who wrote, to whom, in what setting, and for what purpose. The Old Testament provides the scriptural story and promises repeatedly used by Jesus and the New Testament writers. Students should examine every interpretation in its immediate passage and in light of the rest of Scripture.

sections.heading: Four Gospels
sections.content: Luke 1:1–4 says that many had undertaken narratives and that Luke wrote an orderly account after tracing matters carefully. John 20:30–31 explains John's selective purpose. sections.heading: One Creator
sections.content: Genesis 1:1 states that God created the heavens and the earth. Other passages say all things came into being through the Word (John 1:3), that God gives life and breath to all (Acts 17:24–28), and that the seen was not made from things which appear (Hebrews 11:3). “Providence” is a later summary term for biblical statements about God's continuing care and rule, such as Matthew 6:25–34. Students should evaluate the summary from those passages rather than treating the term itself as inspired.

sections.heading: God's Character
sections.content: Isaiah 6 portrays Jehovah as holy and king, exposes Isaiah's uncleanness, provides cleansing, and sends him. Scripture also explicitly describes God as righteous, merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in lovingkindness and truth (for example, Exodus 34:6–7 and Psalm 145:8–17). Saying these qualities belong together is an explanatory conclusion drawn by comparing such passages; each passage should first be heard in its own context.

sections.heading: God's Image
sections.content: Genesis 1:26–28 says God created humanity in his image, male and female, and gave them responsibility within creation. Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 continue to appeal to God's likeness when speaking about human life and speech. Scripture does not give a single dictionary-style definition of the image. Interpretations emphasize representation, relationship, moral capacity, rule, or combinations of these. The clear conclusions are that humans are creatures, owe God obedience, receive a distinctive calling, and must not treat other image-bearers contemptuously.

sections.heading: One God
sections.content: Deuteronomy 6:4 explicitly confesses that Jehovah is one, and the New Testament repeats that there is one God (Mark 12:29; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6). Any explanation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must preserve that scriptural confession rather than teaching three independent gods.

sections.heading: Three Persons
sections.content: The Bible does not use the later phrase “three persons,” but it presents real distinctions: the Father sends the Son (John 3:16–17), the Son speaks to the Father (John 17), and the Spirit is sent, teaches, and bears witness (John 14:16–26; 15:26). At Jesus' baptism the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father's voice speaks (Matthew 3:13–17). “Persons” is explanatory vocabulary used to summarize these distinctions; students should test whether the term accurately serves the passages.

sections.heading: The Word Trinity
sections.content: The word “Trinity” does not appear in Scripture and is not inspired vocabulary. It is a later theological label intended to hold together biblical claims: God is one; the Father is called God; the Word is called God and becomes flesh; and the Holy Spirit is spoken of in divine terms and acts personally (John 1:1–18; Acts 5:3–4). Matthew 28:19 joins Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the singular “name.” The common formulation—one God in three persons—is an interpretation summarizing this combined evidence. It should be evaluated by Scripture, and no analogy should be allowed to override the texts.

sections.heading: The Incarnate Son
sections.content: John 1:1 says the Word was with God and was God; John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Philippians 2:5–11 speaks of Christ existing in the form of God, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness, dying, and receiving universal homage. Hebrews 2:14–18 says he shared flesh and blood. “Incarnation” is a later label meaning becoming flesh. The historic formula “truly God and truly man” is an interpretive summary of these passages, not inspired wording, and must remain answerable to them.

sections.heading: The Kingdom
sections.content: Mark 1:14–15 records Jesus announcing that the time was fulfilled and God's kingdom had drawn near, calling people to repent and believe the gospel. The Gospels connect the kingdom with Jesus' teaching, authority, forgiveness, healings, deliverance, death, and resurrection. Describing the kingdom as God's active rule is an explanatory summary. Jesus' parables show both a present, sometimes hidden work and a future reckoning; students should examine each kingdom passage rather than forcing every text into a single timetable.

sections.heading: Cross and Resurrection

Other passages describe his death using sacrifice, ransom, redemption, reconciliation, covenant, example, and victory over hostile powers. These are biblical images; “atonement theory” is later organization of them. Christians differ over how the images relate, so no one model should silence passages emphasized by another. The cited texts explicitly place Christ's death and bodily resurrection at the center of the gospel.

sections.heading: Sin
sections.content: Romans 1:18–3:23 develops an argument that both Gentiles and Jews are under sin and concludes that all have sinned. Scripture describes sin with several terms and images: lawlessness, transgression, unbelief, corrupt desire, failure to do known good, slavery, and death. “Sin is both acts and a condition or ruling power” is a summary drawn especially from Romans 5–7; students should follow Paul's full argument rather than use one word gloss as a complete doctrine.

sections.heading: Death and Judgment
sections.content: Romans 6:23 contrasts sin's wages, death, with God's gift, eternal life in Christ. Romans 2:1–16 warns against judging others while doing the same things and says God's judgment is according to truth. These texts teach universal accountability and the insufficiency of self-justifying comparison. Explanations of the precise relationship among sin, physical death, spiritual death, and final judgment should be tested across Genesis 2–3, Romans 5–8, and Revelation 20–22.

sections.heading: Good Works
sections.content: Ephesians 2:8–10 says salvation is by grace through faith, not from works for boasting, and immediately says those saved are created in Christ Jesus for good works. Titus 3:3–8 makes the same movement from God's mercy to devoted good works. The conclusion is not that obedience is irrelevant but that it flows from God's saving mercy. Traditions describe the relationship among grace, faith, obedience, and final judgment differently; students should compare Romans 3–4, Galatians 2–3, James 2, and related passages without using one passage to cancel another.

sections.heading: Good News
sections.content: Mark 1:14–15 connects the gospel with God's approaching kingdom and calls for repentance and faith. First Corinthians 15:1–5 summarizes the received gospel around Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances. Gospel translates G2098, euangelion, meaning good news or good tidings. Calling it “news before advice” is an explanatory way to stress that these passages first announce God's action and then call for response.

sections.heading: Grace and Salvation
sections.content: Ephesians 2:1–10 attributes being made alive and saved to God's mercy, love, and grace and excludes boasting. Romans 6 rejects continuing under sin as a proper response to grace. The New Testament uses salvation language for rescue already received, a work presently experienced, and a future completion (Ephesians 2:8; 1 Corinthians 1:18; Romans 13:11). The exact relationship of these uses should be learned from each context.

sections.heading: Gifts of Union with Christ
sections.content: Scripture uses several descriptions of salvation. Romans 3–5 speaks of justification; Romans 5 and 2 Corinthians 5 speak of reconciliation; Romans 8 and Galatians 4 speak of adoption; other passages speak of redemption, forgiveness, new birth, sanctification, and new creation. The brief definitions in this lesson are study summaries, not substitutes for the passages. Traditions differ over how some terms relate, so the student should preserve every biblical image rather than make one term carry the entire doctrine.

sections.heading: Repentance
sections.content: Mark 1:15 joins repentance with believing the gospel. Acts 3:19 calls hearers to repent and turn so sins may be blotted out, and Luke 3 describes fruit worthy of repentance. G3341, metanoia, is commonly translated repentance, but its dictionary gloss alone cannot define the full biblical teaching. The passages show a changed direction involving confession and conduct, not merely regret or self-punishment.

sections.heading: Faith
sections.content: Acts 16:31 calls the jailer to believe on the Lord Jesus. Romans 4 develops Abraham's faith, Romans 10 connects believing with hearing and confession, and James 2 warns against a claimed faith without works. G4102, pistis, can be translated faith, belief, or faithfulness according to context. Interpretations differ over how these passages describe faith's relation to obedience; none should be dismissed before each author's argument is read in full.

sections.heading: Baptism
sections.content: Jesus commands making disciples, baptizing them into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe his commands (Matthew 28:18–20). Acts repeatedly records baptism in response to the gospel. Romans 6:3–4 connects baptism with Christ's death and newness of life; Acts 2:38 connects it with repentance, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit; 1 Peter 3:21 connects it with an appeal to God through Jesus' resurrection. Christians differ over infant or professing-believer baptism, mode, and how baptism relates to regeneration, forgiveness, faith, and assurance. This module does not settle those disputes by selecting one passage and ignoring the others.

sections.heading: The Divine Spirit
sections.content: John 14–16 records the Spirit teaching, reminding, bearing witness, convicting, guiding, and glorifying Christ. Acts 5:3–4 places lying to the Holy Spirit in parallel with lying to God. First Corinthians 12 says the Spirit distributes gifts as he wills. Calling the Spirit personal and divine is an interpretive conclusion drawn from this combined testimony; students should examine the passages and the actions and names they attribute to the Spirit.

sections.heading: Fruit
sections.content: Galatians 5:16–26 contrasts works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, and self-control. The passage places character within walking by the Spirit and belonging to Christ. Dramatic experiences or gifts should not be used to evade this explicit moral test.

sections.heading: Sanctification
sections.content: G38, hagiasmos, is translated sanctification or holiness. First Corinthians 1:2 addresses believers as sanctified in Christ and called saints, while 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8 calls them to continuing holiness. “Already set apart and still growing” summarizes these different uses. sections.heading: Prayer
sections.content: Matthew 6:5–13 records Jesus warning against prayer for public display and teaching prayer for God's name and kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance. Other passages include praise, thanksgiving, confession, lament, intercession, and requests. Saying prayer is communion with God is an explanatory summary. Scripture also shows unanswered or differently answered requests, so prayer should not be presented as a technique for controlling outcomes.

sections.heading: Scripture
sections.content: Second Timothy 3:14–17 says the sacred writings make one wise unto salvation through faith in Christ and equip for every good work. Acts 17:11 praises examining the Scriptures to test teaching. Context, genre, grammar, history, and comparison with other Scripture are study methods serving those texts, not authorities over them. Strong's numbers and lexicons help investigation but cannot prove a doctrine from a gloss alone.

sections.heading: Worship
sections.content: John 4:19–24 records Jesus teaching worship in spirit and truth. Romans 12:1–2 uses worship or service language for presenting the body as a living sacrifice. Acts 2:42 names apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers in the shared life of early believers. The broader description of worship in this lesson is an explanatory collection of scriptural practices, not a command that every gathering follow one denominational order.

sections.heading: A People
sections.content: Acts 2:42–47 describes believers continuing in apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers, shared care, praise, and witness. First Corinthians 12 calls believers Christ's body and members individually; Ephesians 2:19–22 calls them God's household and a holy temple. Ekklesia (G1577) commonly means assembly or congregation. These images describe people joined in Christ, not merely a building or institution.

sections.heading: Leadership and Care
sections.content: Acts 20:17–35, 1 Timothy 3:1–13, Titus 1:5–9, and 1 Peter 5:1–5 describe elders or overseers and servants, emphasizing character, teaching, care, and accountability. Traditions differ over how offices are named, selected, and structured. This lesson does not declare one later polity to be the only possible arrangement; it asks students to compare each model with all relevant passages and to reject domination and exploitation explicitly condemned by Jesus and Peter.

sections.heading: Gifts and Love
sections.content: First Corinthians 12 says gifts come from the same Spirit for the common good and compares the congregation to a body with many necessary members. First Corinthians 13 places love at the center, and chapter 14 emphasizes edification and order. Christians disagree over whether every listed manifestation continues in the same manner. The passages clearly forbid using gifts for superiority or disorder and require that their use build up others.

25. In like manner also the cup, after supper, saying, This cup is the new covenant in my blood: this do, as often as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.

26. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink the cup, ye proclaim the Lord’s death till he come.

27. Wherefore whosoever shall eat the bread or drink the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner, shall be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord.

Study question: What do Jesus and Paul explicitly connect with the bread, the cup, remembrance, participation, unity, self-examination, and Christ's return?

Further reading in context: Luke 22:14–20; 1 Corinthians 10:14–22; 1 Corinthians 11:17–34.

sections.heading: Remember and Proclaim
sections.content: In Luke 22:14–20 Jesus gives the bread and cup in connection with his body and the new covenant in his blood and commands remembrance. First Corinthians 11:23–26 repeats the received tradition and says eating and drinking proclaim the Lord's death until he comes. These explicit statements are the starting point for every explanation of the meal.

sections.heading: Communion
sections.content: First Corinthians 10:16–17 calls the cup a communion or participation in Christ's blood and the bread a communion or participation in Christ's body, then connects the one loaf with the one body. First Corinthians 11 rebukes divisions and humiliation of those who have little. How Christ is present in the meal is disputed, but the passages themselves connect it with Christ, participation, remembrance, proclamation, unity, self-examination, and his return.

sections.heading: Christian Differences
sections.content: The New Testament calls the practice the Lord's supper (1 Corinthians 11:20), breaking of bread (Acts 2:42), and communion or participation (1 Corinthians 10:16). “Eucharist,” from the Greek word for giving thanks, is later common terminology. Traditions differ over Christ's presence, sacramental or ordinance language, who may receive, and frequency. Students should compare those interpretations directly with Matthew 26, Luke 22, and 1 Corinthians 10–11. John 6 is also frequently included in this discussion, although Christians disagree over whether that chapter directly addresses the Lord's Supper.

4. and he shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more: the first things are passed away.

5. And he that sitteth on the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he saith, Write: for these words are faithful and true.

Study question: Separate what the passages clearly affirm from questions of sequence or symbolism that the passages may leave disputed.

Further reading in context: 1 Corinthians 15; Revelation 21–22.

sections.heading: Mission
sections.content: Matthew 28:18–20 records the risen Jesus commanding disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptize them, and teach them to observe his commands. Acts 1:8 speaks of Spirit-empowered witness. The New Testament also commands good works, mercy, truth, and love of neighbor. Describing these together as mission is a study summary; no method may contradict Jesus' commands concerning truth, love, service, and refusal to lord authority over others.

sections.heading: Resurrection and Return
sections.content: First Corinthians 15 argues from Christ's resurrection to the future resurrection of the dead and describes transformation of the body. First Thessalonians 4:13–18 connects hope with the Lord's coming and the raising of the dead in Christ. Scripture clearly affirms Christ's return and resurrection; Christians differ over the sequence and relationship of some end-times passages, so this introduction does not impose a detailed chronology.

sections.heading: Judgment and New Creation
sections.content: Revelation 20:11–15 depicts final judgment, and Revelation 21–22 depicts a new heaven and new earth, God's dwelling with humanity, the removal of death and tears, and the New Jerusalem. Romans 8:18–25 speaks of creation awaiting liberation. Interpretations differ over the symbolism and sequence of apocalyptic passages, but these texts clearly direct hope toward God's final victory, judgment, resurrection life, and renewed creation.

referenceLibrary.title: American Standard Version (ASV)
referenceLibrary.summary: The public-domain 1901 English Bible translation used by this module.
referenceLibrary.content: The American Standard Version was published in 1901 and is in the public domain in the United States. It is a relatively formal English translation and uses older forms such as “thee,” “thou,” and “ye.” In the Old Testament it regularly prints the divine name as “Jehovah.” This module quotes the ASV so its Scripture text can be copied and distributed without a modern publisher license.

referenceLibrary.title: Strong's Numbers
referenceLibrary.summary: An index linking English Bible words to Hebrew and Greek dictionary entries.
referenceLibrary.content: James Strong's 1890 concordance assigned numbers to Hebrew and Greek root entries. An H number refers to the Hebrew dictionary; a G number refers to the Greek dictionary. The number is an index, not part of the inspired text. Strong's brief glosses help beginners locate words, but meaning must be determined from grammar, usage, and context. Modern products bearing the Strong's name may add copyrighted material; this module relies on the original public-domain system.
referenceLibrary.source: James Strong, The Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible (1890)

referenceLibrary.title: Old Testament
referenceLibrary.summary: The Scriptures of Israel received by Christians as the first part of the Bible.
referenceLibrary.content: The Old Testament contains creation and primeval history, the patriarchs, Israel's exodus and covenant, law, historical narratives, poetry, wisdom, prophets, exile, return, and hope. Jesus and the New Testament writers repeatedly appeal to these Scriptures. Different Christian traditions arrange or include some Old Testament writings differently. A later module can examine the history of the biblical canon and those differences in greater detail. This is historical information about canon boundaries, not a ruling by this module; students should distinguish that question from interpreting the content of a biblical passage.

referenceLibrary.title: New Testament
referenceLibrary.summary: Twenty-seven writings centered on Jesus and the apostolic church.
referenceLibrary.content: The New Testament contains four Gospels, Acts, twenty-one letters, and Revelation. All major Christian traditions receive these twenty-seven writings. They bear witness to Jesus Christ, interpret his death and resurrection, describe the church's mission, instruct congregations, and point toward Christ's return and resurrection. This entry describes the collection; claims about its authority should be examined from passages such as 2 Timothy 3:14–17, 2 Peter 3:15–18, and the way Jesus and the apostles use Scripture.

referenceLibrary.title: Gospel
referenceLibrary.summary: Good news about God's saving action through Jesus Christ.
referenceLibrary.content: Gospel translates Strong's G2098, euangelion: good news or good tidings. It can refer to the proclaimed message and, by extension, to the four written Gospel accounts. The gospel announces Jesus' lordship, atoning death, resurrection, and offer of salvation; it calls hearers to repentance, faith, baptism, and discipleship.

referenceLibrary.title: God
referenceLibrary.summary: The one Creator, Lord, and source of all life.
referenceLibrary.content: Genesis 1:1 says God created the heavens and the earth; Deuteronomy 6:4 says Jehovah is one. John 1:3 says all things came into being through the Word, and Acts 17:24–28 says God gives life and breath to all. Strong's H430, Elohim, is a common Hebrew designation translated “God.” H3068 indexes the covenant name printed “Jehovah” in the ASV. These entries help locate usage but do not replace the passages.

referenceLibrary.title: Trinity
referenceLibrary.summary: One God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
referenceLibrary.content: “Trinity” is not a biblical word. It is a later theological label intended to summarize several claims read together: God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4); the Word is with God and is God (John 1:1); the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished and joined within the singular “name” (Matthew 28:19); and the Spirit acts personally and is spoken of in divine terms (John 14–16; Acts 5:3–4). The formulation “one God in three persons” is interpretive, not inspired vocabulary, and must be evaluated by Scripture.

referenceLibrary.title: Holiness
referenceLibrary.summary: God's unique majesty and perfect separation from evil.
referenceLibrary.content: Hebrew H6918, qadosh, and Greek G40, hagios, are commonly translated holy. God is holy in his incomparable divine being and moral purity. People, places, and things are called holy when set apart to God. Christian holiness is received through Christ and lived through Spirit-enabled obedience, not through pride.

referenceLibrary.title: Jesus Christ
referenceLibrary.summary: The incarnate Son, promised Messiah, crucified and risen Lord.
referenceLibrary.content: Jesus is the personal name; Christ comes from G5547, Christos, meaning Anointed One and corresponding to Messiah. The New Testament presents Jesus as truly human and fully sharing the divine identity. His life, kingdom announcement, death for sins, resurrection, ascension, present reign, and return form Christianity's center.

referenceLibrary.title: Incarnation
referenceLibrary.summary: The eternal Son's becoming truly human.
referenceLibrary.content: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Philippians 2:5–11 and Hebrews 2:14–18 describe Christ's divine status, servant form, human likeness, shared flesh and blood, suffering, and death. “Incarnation” is a later label meaning becoming flesh. The historic description “truly God and truly man” is an interpretive summary intended to preserve the combined statements of these passages, not inspired vocabulary.

referenceLibrary.title: Kingdom of God
referenceLibrary.summary: God's active, saving rule made present in Jesus and awaiting fulfillment.
referenceLibrary.content: Jesus announced that God's kingdom had drawn near. His teaching, healings, exorcisms, forgiveness, table fellowship, death, and resurrection display God's reign. The kingdom is already active yet not fully consummated; Christians pray for it to come and live under its values while awaiting Christ's return.

referenceLibrary.title: Atonement
referenceLibrary.summary: Christ's saving work dealing with sin and reconciling people to God.
referenceLibrary.content: “Atonement” is a broad study term for Christ's saving work dealing with sin. The New Testament uses several images: sacrifice, ransom, redemption, justification, reconciliation, covenant, victory over powers, and faithful example. Christians organize these passages into explanations differently. No later model should be used to silence a biblical image emphasized by another passage.

referenceLibrary.title: Sin
referenceLibrary.summary: Rebellion against God and failure to love God and neighbor faithfully.
referenceLibrary.content: G266, hamartia, is the principal Greek entry translated sin. Sin includes acts, desires, omissions, lawlessness, unbelief, injustice, and the deeper condition of alienation from God. Scripture describes all people as sinners needing grace and links sin with guilt, slavery, corruption, judgment, and death.

referenceLibrary.title: Grace
referenceLibrary.summary: God's undeserved favor and generous saving action.
referenceLibrary.content: G5485, charis, is commonly translated grace. Grace is not God pretending evil is harmless; it is God's merciful action toward those unable to save themselves. Grace forgives, justifies, reconciles, adopts, teaches, and transforms. It excludes boasting while creating people for good works.

referenceLibrary.title: Faith
referenceLibrary.summary: Trusting reliance on God and his promise in Jesus Christ.
referenceLibrary.content: G4102, pistis, can express faith, belief, trust, or faithfulness depending on context. Saving faith receives the gospel and entrusts the person to Christ. It is more than awareness of facts and bears fruit in love and obedience. Faith is not confidence in one's own moral record.

referenceLibrary.title: Repentance
referenceLibrary.summary: Turning from sin toward God in a changed mind and life.
referenceLibrary.content: G3341, metanoia, is translated repentance. It involves a change of mind and direction expressed through confession and fitting fruit. Repentance is not merely regret, embarrassment, or self-punishment. It receives mercy and continues as a pattern throughout Christian growth.

referenceLibrary.title: Justification
referenceLibrary.summary: God's gracious act of setting sinners right through faith in Christ.
referenceLibrary.content: G1344, dikaioo, is translated justify and can have declarative or vindicatory senses according to context. Romans 3:21–28 connects justification with grace, Christ's redemption, faith, and exclusion of boasting; Romans 5:1–2 connects it with peace and access. Traditions differ over how justification relates to inward renewal, sacraments, obedience, and final judgment. Romans, Galatians, and James should be compared before adopting a system.

referenceLibrary.title: Reconciliation
referenceLibrary.summary: The restoration of peace between God and sinners through Christ.
referenceLibrary.content: G2643, katallage, refers to reconciliation or restoration to favor. The cross addresses real hostility rather than ignoring it. Reconciled people receive peace with God and become messengers of reconciliation, seeking truthful peace and repair in human relationships.

referenceLibrary.title: Adoption
referenceLibrary.summary: God's welcome of believers into his family as children and heirs.
referenceLibrary.content: Adoption language describes belonging, access, inheritance, discipline, and intimate prayer by the Spirit. Believers become God's children by grace; they do not become divine or become sons in the unique sense in which Jesus is the eternal Son.

referenceLibrary.title: Holy Spirit
referenceLibrary.summary: The divine Spirit who gives life, dwells in believers, and empowers the church.
referenceLibrary.content: John 14–16 portrays the Spirit teaching, reminding, bearing witness, convicting, guiding, and glorifying Christ. Acts 5:3–4 places lying to the Spirit in parallel with lying to God. First Corinthians 12 says the Spirit distributes gifts as he wills, and Galatians 5 describes the Spirit's fruit. Calling the Spirit personal and divine summarizes these texts; the conclusion must remain answerable to them.

referenceLibrary.title: Sanctification
referenceLibrary.summary: Being set apart for God and transformed in holiness.
referenceLibrary.content: G38, hagiasmos, is translated sanctification or holiness. First Corinthians 1:2 speaks of believers as sanctified in Christ; 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8 calls them to continuing sanctification; 2 Corinthians 3:18 speaks of transformation. “Already set apart and continuing to grow” is a summary of these uses. Traditions differ over process and degree, so each passage's context should control.

referenceLibrary.title: Prayer
referenceLibrary.summary: Communion with God through praise, thanks, confession, lament, intercession, and request.
referenceLibrary.content: Jesus' model prayer seeks God's honor and kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance. Prayer is neither magic nor a guarantee that every request will be granted in the requested form. Christians pray in trust, honesty, persistence, and submission to God's wisdom.

referenceLibrary.title: Discipleship
referenceLibrary.summary: Learning from Jesus and living under his lordship.
referenceLibrary.content: A disciple follows Jesus, learns his teaching, shares life with his people, serves others, and helps make disciples. Discipleship includes a cross: allegiance to Jesus can be costly. This obedience responds to grace rather than purchasing salvation.

referenceLibrary.title: Baptism
referenceLibrary.summary: The water rite Jesus commanded at the beginning of discipleship.
referenceLibrary.content: Matthew 28:18–20 commands baptism. Acts 2:38 connects it with repentance, forgiveness, and the gift of the Spirit; Romans 6:3–4 connects it with Christ's death and newness of life; 1 Peter 3:21 connects it with an appeal to God through Jesus' resurrection. Christians differ over infant or professing-believer baptism, mode, and how baptism relates to regeneration, forgiveness, faith, and assurance. This entry preserves the relevant texts without selecting one denominational conclusion.

referenceLibrary.title: Church
referenceLibrary.summary: The community called by God in Christ to worship, learn, serve, and witness.
referenceLibrary.content: G1577, ekklesia, means assembly or congregation. The church is described as Christ's body, God's household, and a holy temple. Local churches gather around apostolic teaching, fellowship, prayer, baptism, the Lord's Supper, service, discipline, and mission.

referenceLibrary.title: Lord's Supper
referenceLibrary.summary: The meal Jesus gave the church to remember and proclaim his death.
referenceLibrary.content: Luke 22:14–20 connects bread and the cup with Jesus' body and new-covenant blood and commands remembrance. First Corinthians 10:16–17 speaks of communion or participation in Christ's body and blood and connects one loaf with one body. First Corinthians 11:23–26 says the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes. Traditions differ over Christ's presence, sacramental or ordinance language, admission, and frequency; the texts are primary.

referenceLibrary.title: Spiritual Gifts
referenceLibrary.summary: Spirit-given abilities and ministries for the church's common good.
referenceLibrary.content: First Corinthians 12 says manifestations of the Spirit are given for the common good and compares the congregation to a body. Chapters 13–14 require love, edification, and order. Romans 12:3–8 and 1 Peter 4:10–11 add further gifts. Christians differ over whether every listed manifestation continues in the same manner today. The passages clearly direct gifts toward service rather than status.

referenceLibrary.title: Resurrection
referenceLibrary.summary: God's raising of the dead, grounded in Jesus' bodily resurrection.
referenceLibrary.content: Jesus' resurrection is central to the gospel and the beginning of new creation. Christian hope is not merely the soul's survival after death; it includes the future resurrection and transformation of the body. Paul calls death the last enemy to be abolished.

referenceLibrary.title: Final Judgment
referenceLibrary.summary: God's just exposure and judgment of evil through Jesus Christ.
referenceLibrary.content: Acts 17:30–31 says God commands repentance and has appointed a day to judge through the risen Jesus. Romans 2:1–16 speaks of judgment according to truth and without partiality. Revelation 20:11–15 depicts final judgment. Christians debate the sequence and interpretation of some judgment passages, but these texts plainly present accountability to God and his final judgment.

referenceLibrary.title: New Creation
referenceLibrary.summary: The promised renewal in which God dwells with his people and death is no more.
referenceLibrary.content: Isaiah 65:17–25 speaks of new heavens and a new earth. Romans 8:18–25 describes creation awaiting liberation, and Revelation 21–22 depicts a new heaven and earth, God's dwelling with humanity, tears removed, and death no more. “New creation” summarizes these passages. Interpretations differ over prophetic and apocalyptic details, so the imagery and context of each text should be studied directly.

referenceLibrary.title: Textual Variants and Translation Differences
referenceLibrary.summary: Why ancient Bible manuscripts sometimes differ and how responsible study handles the evidence.
referenceLibrary.content: The biblical books were copied by hand for centuries, and surviving manuscripts contain differences in spelling, word order, omitted or repeated words, and a smaller number of longer disputed passages. Modern translations may place brackets or footnotes at Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11 because the earliest and strongest manuscript evidence does not contain them in those locations. The longer wording commonly associated with 1 John 5:7 also lacks early Greek manuscript support. These facts should be stated honestly rather than hidden. Most variants are minor, and central teachings such as God's identity, Jesus' deity and humanity, his death, bodily resurrection, salvation through him, and resurrection hope are taught in many unaffected passages. Students should compare translations, read textual footnotes, examine the surrounding context, and avoid building a doctrine on a disputed wording alone.
referenceLibrary.source: Compare ASV textual notes and the manuscript notes in responsibly edited Greek New Testaments; examine Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11, and 1 John 5:7 in multiple translations.

editorialStandard.name: RoadReady Bible Module Editorial Standard
editorialStandard.authorityStatement: Scripture is the primary authority. Commentary, historical terminology, and study tools are subordinate and should be tested against the biblical text.
editorialStandard.bereanPrinciple: Examine the Scriptures to test every teaching, including this module (Acts 17:11).
contentApproach: Present the cited biblical passages before explanatory commentary.
Identify later theological vocabulary as uninspired study terminology.
Distinguish explicit biblical statements from interpretive synthesis.
Present major interpretations fairly on disputed secondary issues.
Use original-language tools to clarify context, never to prove doctrine from a gloss alone.
